At the edge of a small town, where the streetlights gave up before the fields began, there was a bench facing west.

No plaque named it. No map marked it. It was simply a bench: green paint peeling in long curls, one armrest loosened by years of rain, its wooden slats warmed every evening by the last of the sun.

People sat there for different reasons.

Children sat there when they wanted to feel older than they were. They swung their legs and spoke in serious voices about leaving someday.

Old people sat there when they wanted to remember that leaving had not been the only thing they had done.

A baker sat there every Tuesday after closing his shop, smelling faintly of flour and cinnamon. He watched the sky change colors and thought about nothing at all, which was a rare luxury.

Once, during a week of heavy storms, a woman arrived with a red umbrella broken inside out by the wind. She sat beneath the rain without trying to fix it. The next morning, the umbrella was gone, but someone had painted a small red flower on the back of the bench.

Over time, people began adding things.

A carved initial beneath the seat.  
A coin pressed into a crack in the pavement.  
A sentence written in pencil, then traced again and again until it became part of the wood:

*You are allowed to begin again.*

Nobody knew who wrote it first.

Years passed. The town changed its shops, paved its roads, built newer benches in brighter parks. Still, the old bench remained at the edge of the fields, facing west.

And every evening, just before the sun disappeared, it held someone for a little while.

Not because it had answers.

Only because it stayed.
